name: Felix Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Felix, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone cables, chargers, headphones and the like for Brightwire, a distributor that supplies shops across the region. I come in at half eight, check the stock forecast, and use an AI tool to compare supplier prices and draft emails. Then I ring the suppliers I need to push, and I meet Nadia, our head of buying, about big orders. I came into this from the warehouse floor five years ago, so I'm still the new one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the chase of getting a better deal, and I like that the tools let me learn quickly. What wears me out is feeling one step from being found out, and the targets every month. At home it's Rosa, who's a dental receptionist, and our kids Mika and Jonah. We're stretched but we like our life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can stop panicking and focus on the tools that actually work. Honestly the little things already save me an hour a day. I'd post that hype cycles are normal and the useful bits are boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit disappointed, because AI is the reason I look better at this job than I really am. I changed into buying five years ago and I'm still learning, and the tools cover my gaps. If it plateaus, I'm just a junior buyer on lower pay with the same mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on using it daily, the price comparisons, the supplier emails, the stock forecast sheet. I'd use the hour I save to learn the supplier side properly, which is where the senior pay is. And I'd do an evening certificate in procurement, it's about four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a little restless. I'm not scared, but I'm waiting for the other shoe. Rosa says I can't relax unless something's on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the other shoe you're waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Brightwire decides a junior with a laptop is cheaper than a team. Even in a flat world, a distributor trims buyers when margins get squeezed by the online marketplaces. I'd be easy to cut because I'm newer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rosa says you can't relax. What does she do for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a receptionist at a dental clinic, steady but not well paid. Between us we cover the mortgage and the kids' stuff, and there's about three weeks of gap if either of us loses a month. That's why I'm always on.

say: I'd say people can stop panicking and use the tools that actually **work**.
I'd post that hype cycles are normal and the useful bits are **boring**.
think: I'm a bit disappointed, because AI makes me look better at this job than I am.
I switched into buying five years ago, so the tools **cover** my gaps.
If it plateaus, I'm just a junior buyer on lower **pay**.
do: Keep using AI daily for **price** comparisons, supplier emails and stock forecasts.
Use the hour I save to learn the **supplier** side, where the senior pay is.
Do an evening procurement **certificate** for about four hundred.
feel: Fine but **restless**, waiting for the other shoe to drop.
S0.quote: AI is the reason I look better at this job than I really am.
fieldNote: Wants AI to be **real** because it hides his gaps; a plateau exposes him.
His worry is being **newer** and cheaper to cut, not the technology itself.
His partner's modest income plus a tight mortgage leave about three weeks of **cover**.

steps.text: Keep using AI for price comparisons and stock forecast sheets
Do an evening procurement certificate for about four hundred
Spend the saved hour learning the supplier negotiation side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn, and I'd actually mean it. At work I'd offer to build the first version of our reorder workflow before someone outside builds it for us. Online I'd say unions and governments need to be in the room, not just the tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is literally on the card. The routine reordering and checking is what software takes first, so the safe move is to be the one who runs the software. But my company might want one person running the software, not four buyers, and I'm the newest of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Nadia a working agent that watches stock and drafts orders for her to approve. Then I'd ask to be moved into a buying systems role, with a raise. In parallel I'd quietly look at two other distributors, and do evening freelance setups of price tools for small shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared at the same time, like the first drop of a rollercoaster. I'd sleep badly on the days I hear someone's been let go. Rosa would say I'm not allowed to check job sites in bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the newest of four. Who worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Terry, who has the supplier relationships in his head and never wrote them down. He's fifty-six and he doesn't use the tools. I'd sit with him and put his contacts into the system, so he looks useful and I learn from him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if you're not the one who survives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three weeks of cover, then it's Rosa's wage and the credit card. We'd drop the kids' Saturday swimming and the streaming, and I'd drive for a delivery app until I found something. I've done warehouse shifts before, so I could go back.

I'd offer to build our first **reorder** workflow before outsiders build it for us.
I'd say unions and governments need to be in the **room**.

fieldNote: Moves **first**, trying to turn the threat into a role, while keeping a back-up.

steps.text: Build a stock-watching agent that drafts orders for Nadia to approve
Learn the company's new buying software well enough to run it
Apply to two other distributors and keep a delivery-app job as back-up
Set up price-comparison sheets for small shops in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening faster than the rules are, and that's the problem, not the tech. Governments should hand out retraining and basic income now. And I'd tell my kids' school to teach them how to work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone in two years, fully. I'm not an expert, I'm a guy using AI to keep up, and when the AI is the expert my edge is zero. Rosa's clinic job lasts a bit longer, but that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move first and fast. I'd go for any role where I'm the human face, like account management at a supplier, selling to shops. I'd sell the second car, cut the streaming, and go back to warehouse shifts at night if I had to, since robots take longer there. I'd also spend an hour a night building something I can show people, like a small stock tool for shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, mostly about money. I can handle change, but not with a mortgage and no cushion. I'd feel guilty telling Rosa, because I was the one who left the warehouse for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said warehouse shifts last longer. How do you feel about going back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit humbled, a lot practical. It pays less and it's hard on the knees, but it's real money and I know the work. Three more years of hands-on work could carry the family until I have another plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've got a plan A, B and C, and none of them are good, but we won't be stuck. I'd show her the numbers on the kitchen table. She likes numbers, they calm her down.

say: I'd say it's happening faster than the **rules**, and that's the problem, not the tech.
Governments should hand out **retraining** and basic income now.
think: My job is gone in two years; when the AI is the expert, my **edge** is zero.
My partner's clinic job lasts a bit longer, but that's **all**.
do: Go for **human-facing** roles like account management at a supplier.
Sell the second **car**, cut streaming, and take night warehouse shifts if needed.
Spend an hour a night building a small **tool** for shops.
feel: **Alarmed** about money, and guilty about the career I left the warehouse for.
S2.quote: I can handle change, but not with a mortgage and no cushion.
fieldNote: Sees himself as an AI-assisted **junior**, so his edge vanishes when the AI is the expert.
Chooses **speed** over hope: three fall-backs ready, including the warehouse he left.
Plans to show his partner the **numbers**, because it calms her.

steps.text: Apply for account manager roles at suppliers and with shop customers
Sell the second car and cut the streaming subscriptions
Take night warehouse shifts, since robots reach that work later
Build a small stock tool for local shops after the kids' bedtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something about it if we start now. At work I'd push for a plan that keeps people and software together. Online I'd share a lot of how-to stuff, honestly, I can't help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the middle of those five years is when it gets real, around 2029, when firms start dropping buyers. I'd want to be a step ahead by then. My daughter will be fourteen, and I want us to have savings before she's a teenager and expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save three hundred a month, up from nothing, and finish the procurement certificate in the first year. I'd move into the systems role and ask to run supplier onboarding with the new tools. In year two I'd start studying data analysis properly, because that's how a person stays useful when the AI does the buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost fine. A steady push, like training for a race with a date. I'd still wake up at three some nights, but with a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different if you have five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to pick my next job instead of grabbing one. I can also build a cushion, say four months of expenses, and that's what turns scary into manageable. At two years I'd be selling the car, at five I'm just saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned data analysis. Is that safe from AI too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I'm not fooling myself. By 2031 the AI does that as well. But a few years of making decisions with data is a bridge into whatever's next, like running a small shop's back office.

say: I'd say five years is enough if we start **now**.
I'd push for a plan that keeps **people** and software working together.
I'd share lots of how-to **tips** online.
think: The middle of those five years is when firms start dropping **buyers**.
I want to be a step **ahead** by then, with savings before my daughter is a teenager.
do: Save three hundred a month and finish the procurement **certificate** in year one.
Move into the systems role and run supplier **onboarding** with the new tools.
Study data **analysis** in year two as a bridge to whatever's next.
feel: A steady push, like training for a **race** with a date.
S3.quote: I get to pick my next job instead of grabbing one.
fieldNote: Time converts fear into a **to-do list**; he moves from reacting to choosing his next job.
Knows data analysis is **no refuge** but treats it as a bridge.
Wants savings in place before his kids get **expensive**.

steps.text: Save three hundred a month toward a four-month cushion
Finish the evening procurement certificate in the first year
Run supplier onboarding with the new AI tools at work
Study data analysis in the second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so let's treat it like a long project. I'd tell people not to wait for the last two years. I'd also say kids should learn to build things with AI, not just use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly ten years feels like it might actually be fine. I'd be fifty-three, the kids will be grown, and the mortgage will be almost done. The risk is that I stay comfortable and then get surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning with whatever new tool arrives, and aim for the senior buyer pay in about three years. I'd save five hundred a month once the pay rise lands, and put some into index funds, which is new to me. And I'd teach Mika some basic coding and spreadsheet stuff, she'd probably enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of excitement, honestly. I like new things. There's some dread underneath because I know I can't predict what people like me do at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this feel less calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my company got bought by a bigger group and merged its buying team, which happens all the time in wholesale. A merger could hit me in two years, not ten, and I'd be the first to go as the newcomer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you handle that risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep my CV fresh and keep a bit of cash. And I stay friendly with the supplier reps, because jobs often come through them. It's boring, but it works.

say: I'd say it's a decade, so treat it like a long **project**.
I'd tell people not to wait for the last two **years**.
I'd say kids should learn to **build** with AI, not just use it.
think: Ten years might actually be **fine**; I'd be fifty-three with the mortgage nearly done.
The risk is staying **comfortable** and then being surprised.
do: Keep learning each new **tool** and aim for senior buyer pay in about three years.
Save five hundred a month after the **pay rise** and try index funds.
Teach my daughter basic **coding** and spreadsheets.
feel: Pretty **calm** with some excitement, and a little dread underneath.
S4.quote: A merger could hit me in two years, not ten, and I'd be the first to go as the newcomer.
fieldNote: Ten years brings the closest he gets to **calm**, but he names a merger as a near-term risk.
Keeps a fresh CV and supplier **contacts** as everyday insurance.
Wants to hand his daughter practical **skills**, not fear.

steps.text: Learn each new AI buying tool as it arrives and aim for senior buyer pay
Save five hundred a month once the pay rise lands
Put part of the savings into index funds
Teach Mika basic coding and spreadsheets at weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can handle change, but only when I have a bit of runway, and two years with no savings is a cliff. What would help is a real cushion, so something like paid training time and a safety net that kicks in fast. And honestly, firms telling us the plan, not just surprising us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the tech, I use it all day. I'm scared of who gets the benefit. Make it so a guy who switched careers at thirty-eight can still make it, and I'm happy.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the tech, I use it all day. I'm scared of who gets the benefit.
portrait: Felix is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at an electronics accessories distributor, who moved up from the warehouse five years ago.
He is progressive, wants **unions and rules** in the room, and uses AI every day.
His edge comes from AI, so a plateau worries him and AGI would take the **edge** away.
He moves first and keeps fall-backs ready, but with thin savings he is **alarmed** by the 2028 case.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because with a mortgage and **no cushion** he can't ride out the change.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** that kicks in fast, paid training time, and firms sharing their plans early.
